cards.front: Beds {{c1::in parallel}} are fed side by side from the same arteries and drain into the same veins, so they share one driving pressure.
cards.quote: Beds in parallel are fed side by side from the same arteries and drain into the same veins, so they share one driving pressure.

cards.front: In the fetal circulation, what rule decides how blood divides among parallel beds, and which way it crosses an open shunt?
cards.back: Blood divides among parallel beds in proportion to how easily each lets it through; where two chambers or vessels connect, it crosses from higher pressure to lower.
cards.quote: Blood divides among beds in parallel in proportion to how easily each one lets it through

cards.front: Once the newborn's shunts close, why do the lungs carry the whole output of the right ventricle whatever their resistance?
cards.back: With no shunt to bypass them, the lungs sit in series with the body, so all right ventricular output must pass through them.
cards.why: Resistance decides how flow divides only among beds in parallel; in series, every bed carries the full flow.
cards.quote: Once the shunts close, the lungs sit in series with the body and carry the whole output of the right ventricle, whatever their resistance.

cards.front: In the human placenta, each fetal villus is covered by the {{c1::syncytiotrophoblast}}, a continuous multinucleated layer with no gaps between cells.
cards.back: Everything moving between mother and fetus crosses it and the fetal capillary wall; the two bloods normally do not mix.
cards.quote: covered by the syncytiotrophoblast, a continuous multinucleated layer with no gaps between cells
cards.section: The placenta: the fetus's lung, gut and kidney

cards.front: Across the human placenta, glucose moves down a maternal-to-fetal concentration gradient by {{c1::facilitated diffusion}}, mainly through GLUT1.
cards.quote: Glucose moves down a maternal-to-fetal concentration gradient by facilitated diffusion, mainly through the transporter GLUT1.
cards.section: The placenta: the fetus's lung, gut and kidney

cards.front: Why can amino acid transfer from mother to fetus not be simple diffusion, and how is it done?
cards.back: Several amino acids are more concentrated in fetal than maternal plasma, so they move against their gradient, carried by transporters in both syncytiotrophoblast membranes, two steps in series.
cards.quote: Amino acids still move from mother to fetus, but against their gradient: several are more concentrated in fetal than maternal plasma.
cards.section: The placenta: the fetus's lung, gut and kidney

cards.front: Suppose fetal hemoglobin bound oxygen no more tightly than adult hemoglobin. At the PO2 reached in the placenta, what would happen to fetal oxygen loading, and why?
cards.back: Fetal blood would carry less oxygen at that PO2. Oxygen crosses by diffusion down its PO2 gradient, and the higher affinity of fetal hemoglobin is what lets fetal blood hold more oxygen at a given PO2.
cards.quote: fetal hemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly at a given PO2 than adult hemoglobin does
cards.section: The placenta: the fetus's lung, gut and kidney

cards.front: What does human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) do early in pregnancy, and why does that matter?
cards.back: It supports the maternal corpus luteum, so progesterone production continues past the point where the luteum would regress, until the placenta becomes the main source.
cards.quote: supports the maternal corpus luteum, so progesterone production continues past the point where the luteum would otherwise regress
cards.section: The placenta is also an endocrine organ

cards.front: In pregnancy, what does progesterone do to the myometrium, and through what kind of receptor?
cards.back: It promotes quiescence of the myometrium, acting through its nuclear receptor.
cards.quote: Progesterone acts through its nuclear receptor (nuclear receptors) and promotes quiescence of the myometrium
cards.section: The placenta is also an endocrine organ

cards.front: Why can the human placenta not make estrogens on its own, and how does it get around this?
cards.back: It lacks 17α-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase, so it cannot make androgen precursors. It converts DHEAS from maternal and fetal adrenals into estrogens: the maternal-fetal-placental unit.
cards.quote: The placenta lacks the enzyme that turns progesterone-type steroids into androgens (17α-hydroxylase/17,20-lyase), so it cannot make the androgen precursors that estrogens are built from.
cards.section: The placenta is also an endocrine organ

cards.front: Why does the mother become insulin resistant in the second half of pregnancy, and which placental hormones are the likely drivers?
cards.back: It spares glucose for the fetus: her tissues take up less, so more stays in her blood. Likely drivers are human placental lactogen (hPL) and placental growth hormone.
cards.quote: In the second half of pregnancy the mother becomes insulin resistant, an adaptation that spares glucose for the fetus.
cards.section: The placenta is also an endocrine organ

cards.front: A pregnant woman develops normal maternal insulin resistance of late pregnancy, but her insulin secretion does not rise. What happens to her blood glucose, and what is the condition?
cards.back: Blood glucose rises: gestational diabetes. Normally insulin secretion rises, with beta-cell expansion, to compensate for the resistance.
cards.quote: If insulin secretion does not rise enough to match the resistance, blood glucose rises: that is gestational diabetes
cards.section: The placenta is also an endocrine organ

cards.front: In healthy human pregnancy, cardiac output rises by around {{c1::40 percent}}, yet mean arterial pressure changes only slightly.
cards.quote: in healthy human pregnancy, cardiac output rises by around 40 percent, yet mean arterial pressure changes only slightly
cards.section: The mother re-sets her circulation, breathing and kidneys

cards.front: Made-up example: before pregnancy a woman's mean arterial pressure is 90 mmHg and cardiac output 5.0 L per min (right atrial pressure taken as 0). In pregnancy cardiac output rises 40 percent and systemic vascular resistance falls 25 percent. What is her mean arterial pressure?
cards.back: SVR = 90 / 5.0 = 18.0 mmHg min per L; new SVR = 18.0 × 0.75 = 13.5. CO = 7.0 L per min. MAP = 7.0 × 13.5 = 94.5 mmHg.
cards.why: MAP = CO × SVR: the rise in output is largely cancelled by the fall in resistance.
cards.quote: At the edges of that range, a 25 percent fall gives 94.5 mmHg and a 30 percent fall gives 88.2 mmHg.
cards.section: The mother re-sets her circulation, breathing and kidneys

cards.front: If cardiac output rises 1.4-fold in pregnancy, to what fraction of its old value must systemic vascular resistance fall for mean arterial pressure to stay exactly unchanged?
cards.back: 1 / 1.4 = 0.714, a fall of about 29 percent. The reported fall to about 0.72 is close to this reciprocal, so pressure barely moves.
cards.why: MAP = CO × SVR; holding MAP fixed requires SVR to change by the reciprocal of CO.
cards.quote: her resistance falls to about 0.72 of its old value, close to the reciprocal of the 1.4-fold rise in her output
cards.section: Milk: prolactin fills, oxytocin empties

cards.front: In pregnancy, is the fall in maternal systemic vascular resistance mainly caused by the placenta? Explain.
cards.back: No. Resistance falls in the first weeks, before the uteroplacental bed is large, through body-wide vasodilation (nitric oxide and hormonal signals). Even at term other beds, such as kidney and skin, account for much of it.
cards.quote: Resistance falls in the first weeks, before the uteroplacental bed is large, through vasodilation
cards.section: The mother re-sets her circulation, breathing and kidneys

cards.front: Why does hemoglobin concentration fall in healthy pregnancy?
cards.back: By dilution: plasma volume expands proportionally more than red-cell mass. Red cells are not lost.
cards.quote: Plasma volume expands proportionally more than red-cell mass, so hemoglobin concentration falls by dilution rather than because red cells were lost
cards.section: The mother re-sets her circulation, breathing and kidneys

cards.front: Made-up example: before pregnancy, plasma volume is 2.6 L and red-cell volume 1.4 L. In pregnancy plasma rises 50 percent and red cells 25 percent. Give hematocrit before and after.
cards.back: Before: 1.4 / 4.0 = 35.0 percent. After: plasma 3.9 L, red cells 1.75 L, blood 5.65 L; hematocrit 1.75 / 5.65 = 31.0 percent, lower by dilution.
cards.quote: Hematocrit is the fraction of blood volume taken up by red cells.
cards.section: The mother re-sets her circulation, breathing and kidneys

cards.front: Made-up example: in pregnancy hematocrit falls from 37.5 to 33.3 percent while cardiac output rises 40 percent. Hemoglobin per litre of red cells and saturation are unchanged; ignore dissolved oxygen. How does oxygen delivery change?
cards.back: Content scales with hematocrit: 33.3 / 37.5 = 0.889. Delivery = 1.40 × 0.889 = 1.24, about 24 percent higher although content is about 11 percent lower.
cards.quote: Delivery is about 24 percent higher although content is about 11 percent lower.
cards.section: The mother re-sets her circulation, breathing and kidneys

cards.front: In healthy human pregnancy, minute ventilation rises by up to about 48 percent in the first trimester. Through tidal volume or respiratory rate?
cards.back: Larger tidal volumes, at an essentially unchanged respiratory rate.
cards.quote: It rises through larger tidal volumes at an essentially unchanged respiratory rate.
cards.section: The mother re-sets her circulation, breathing and kidneys

cards.front: Why does maternal arterial PCO2 settle around 32 mmHg in pregnancy?
cards.back: Progesterone raises the sensitivity of the respiratory centre to carbon dioxide, so she ventilates more and PCO2 settles at a lower plateau.
cards.quote: Progesterone raises the sensitivity of the respiratory centre to carbon dioxide (control of breathing), so arterial PCO2 settles at a plateau around 32 mmHg.
cards.section: The mother re-sets her circulation, breathing and kidneys

cards.front: Made-up example: arterial PCO2 starts at 40 mmHg and CO2 production rises 10 percent. By what factor must alveolar ventilation rise for steady-state PCO2 to settle at 32 mmHg?
cards.back: PCO2 is proportional to CO2 production / alveolar ventilation. Factor = 1.10 × 40 / 32 = 1.375, a rise of 37.5 percent. Check: 40 × 1.10 / 1.375 = 32 mmHg.
cards.quote: In the steady state, arterial PCO2 is proportional to CO2 production divided by alveolar ventilation.
cards.section: The mother re-sets her circulation, breathing and kidneys

cards.front: What does the lower maternal arterial PCO2 of pregnancy do for the fetus?
cards.back: It steepens the gradient that carries fetal CO2 across the placenta.
cards.quote: a lower maternal PCO2 steepens the gradient that carries fetal CO2 across the placenta
cards.section: The mother re-sets her circulation, breathing and kidneys

cards.front: In pregnancy, {{c1::functional residual capacity}} falls as the diaphragm is displaced upward.
cards.quote: Functional residual capacity falls as the diaphragm is displaced upward.
cards.section: The mother re-sets her circulation, breathing and kidneys

cards.front: Glomerular filtration rate rises by up to 40 to 50 percent early in healthy pregnancy. Predict the change in serum creatinine, and why.
cards.back: It falls: faster filtration clears creatinine faster. In pooled data it was lowest at 15 to 21 weeks, 23.2 percent below nonpregnant values.
cards.quote: Glomerular filtration rate is already up to 40 to 50 percent higher in the first trimester.
cards.section: The mother re-sets her circulation, breathing and kidneys

cards.front: Why are the fetal lungs a high-resistance bed while the placenta is a low-resistance one?
cards.back: The lungs are fluid-filled; their small arteries are held constricted by low oxygen and compressed by lung liquid. The placenta is a wide, low-resistance bed.
cards.quote: The fluid-filled lungs, whose small arteries are held constricted by low oxygen and compressed by lung liquid, are a high-resistance bed.
cards.section: Where fetal blood goes

cards.front: In the fetus, which vessel carries the best-oxygenated blood?
cards.back: The umbilical vein, returning from the placenta.
cards.quote: Oxygenated blood returns in the umbilical vein.
cards.section: Where fetal blood goes

cards.front: In the fetus, what does the ductus venosus carry, and to where?
cards.back: A variable share of umbilical venous blood, past the liver, toward the inferior vena cava. The rest perfuses the liver.
cards.quote: A variable share of it runs through the ductus venosus, past the liver, toward the inferior vena cava
cards.section: Where fetal blood goes

cards.front: At the fetal foramen ovale, a flap on the left side lets blood through only from {{c1::right to left}}, like a door that opens one way.
cards.quote: A flap on the left side of the opening lets blood through only from right to left, like a door that opens one way.
cards.section: Where fetal blood goes

cards.front: In the fetus, why does most right ventricular output go through the ductus arteriosus, and in which direction?
cards.back: The fluid-filled lungs offer high resistance, so most blood leaving the right ventricle goes from the pulmonary artery through the ductus into the aorta.
cards.quote: There it meets the high resistance of the lungs, and most of it takes a short vessel, the ductus arteriosus, into the aorta.
cards.section: Where fetal blood goes

cards.front: What mainly holds the fetal ductus arteriosus open, and where does it come from?
cards.back: Prostaglandin E2, much of it made by the placenta and some by the ductal wall; nitric oxide also contributes.
cards.quote: The ductus is held open mainly by prostaglandin E2, much of it made by the placenta and some by the ductal wall itself
cards.section: Where fetal blood goes

cards.front: In the fetus, the first aortic branches feed the heart muscle and head, and the ductus arteriosus joins the aorta after them. Which blood does the brain mostly get?
cards.back: The better-oxygenated stream that crossed the foramen ovale and left via the left ventricle. Less-oxygenated right ventricular blood enters downstream through the ductus and goes to the lower body and placenta.
cards.quote: The first branches of the aorta feed the heart muscle and the head, and the ductus arteriosus joins the aorta after those branches.
cards.section: Where fetal blood goes

cards.front: At birth, why does pulmonary vascular resistance fall?
cards.back: The first breaths fill the lungs with air; the air and the rise in oxygen relax the small pulmonary arteries, and resistance falls several-fold.
cards.quote: the air and the rise in oxygen relax the small pulmonary arteries, and pulmonary vascular resistance falls several-fold
cards.section: At birth the lungs and the placenta trade places

cards.front: At birth, why does losing the placenta raise systemic vascular resistance?
cards.back: The placenta was a low-resistance bed in parallel with the body. Removing it removes that easy circuit, so systemic resistance and ventricular afterload rise.
cards.quote: Losing the placental bed removes a low-resistance circuit, so systemic vascular resistance and ventricular afterload
cards.section: At birth the lungs and the placenta trade places

cards.front: In the first hours after birth the ductus arteriosus is still open. Which way does blood now flow through it, and why?
cards.back: Mostly aorta to pulmonary artery (often both ways on day 1). Pulmonary resistance falls below systemic, so aortic pressure exceeds pulmonary artery pressure, and blood crosses from higher to lower pressure.
cards.quote: As pulmonary resistance falls below systemic, aortic pressure exceeds pulmonary artery pressure, and the open ductus carries blood from higher pressure to lower.
cards.section: At birth the lungs and the placenta trade places

cards.front: After the first breaths, what happens to left and right atrial pressures, and what does that do at the foramen ovale?
cards.back: Left atrial pressure rises (more pulmonary venous return); right falls (umbilical return gone). Left now exceeds right, so the one-way flap is pressed shut and right-to-left flow stops.
cards.quote: Once left atrial pressure exceeds right, the one-way flap is pressed against the opening and the foramen ovale stops carrying a right-to-left stream.
cards.section: At birth the lungs and the placenta trade places

cards.front: A pressure reversal turns flow in the newborn ductus arteriosus around but does not close it. What closes it?
cards.back: Its smooth muscle constricts as its blood becomes well oxygenated, and prostaglandin E2 falls because the placenta is gone and the newly perfused lungs break it down.
cards.quote: Its smooth muscle constricts as the blood in it becomes well oxygenated (smooth muscle), and the prostaglandin E2 that held it open falls
cards.section: At birth the lungs and the placenta trade places

cards.front: An infant's ductus arteriosus stays open after birth. A drug that blocks prostaglandin synthesis, such as indomethacin, is given. What happens, and why?
cards.back: The ductus closes. Prostaglandin E2 holds it open, so blocking its synthesis removes the dilator. Conversely, prostaglandin E1 is used to keep a ductus open.
cards.quote: drugs that block prostaglandin synthesis, such as indomethacin and ibuprofen, are used to close a ductus that stays open
cards.section: Closing the ductus

cards.front: In healthy term babies, roughly when do the ductus arteriosus and ductus venosus stop carrying flow, and how often does the foramen ovale never fully seal?
cards.back: Ductus arteriosus mostly before day 3; ductus venosus by day 18. The foramen ovale never fully seals in about a quarter of adults.
cards.quote: in about a quarter of adults the foramen ovale never fully seals
cards.section: At birth the lungs and the placenta trade places

cards.front: In persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn, pulmonary vascular resistance fails to fall. Predict flow at the foramen ovale and ductus arteriosus, and the effect on the duct's closure.
cards.back: Both shunts keep the fetal pattern: low pulmonary flow keeps left atrial pressure low, so right atrial pressure can remain higher and foramen ovale flow stays right to left; pulmonary pressure can stay at or above aortic, sending ductal flow toward the aorta. Low systemic PO2 removes one constricting stimulus.
cards.why: Same rule run backwards: blood crosses from higher pressure to lower.
cards.quote: Systemic arterial PO2 stays low, removing one stimulus that constricts the duct.
cards.section: At birth the lungs and the placenta trade places

cards.front: In preterm lambs, clamping the cord before aerating the lungs cut right ventricular output by about two-thirds; ventilating first kept output largely steady. What is the likely reading, and what can the experiment not separate?
cards.back: The heart lost umbilical venous return, much of its preload, before pulmonary venous return could take over. It cannot separate this from a lost placental transfusion of blood volume. Preterm lambs, no human outcome.
cards.quote: In preterm lambs, right ventricular output fell by about two-thirds.
cards.section: At birth the lungs and the placenta trade places

cards.front: In the clamp-first preterm lambs, right ventricular output fell from 114.6 to 38.8 mL per min per kg while heart rate fell about 40 percent. By about how much did stroke volume fall?
cards.back: Output ratio 38.8 / 114.6 = 0.339. Stroke volume ratio = 0.339 / 0.60 = 0.56, a fall of about 44 percent. Both rate and stroke volume fell.
cards.why: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume, so the output fall is not purely a stroke-volume effect.
cards.quote: Heart rate was also down by about 40 percent, so the fall in output is not purely a stroke-volume effect
cards.section: Clamp first or breathe first

cards.front: Ventilating preterm lambs before clamping the cord preserves right ventricular output. Design groups to tell whether pulmonary venous return supplies replacement preload or the placenta transfuses blood volume.
cards.back: Compare clamp-then-ventilate, ventilate-then-clamp, ventilate-first with the umbilical vein occluded, and clamp-first plus measured transfusion, with a tracer blood-volume measure. Preload: vein-occluded group keeps output. Transfusion: it loses the benefit.
cards.quote: ventilate first with the umbilical vein occluded for the same interval, so no placental blood can return
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In humans, unlike sheep, circulating progesterone stays high until birth. How is its block on the uterus thought to be lifted?
cards.back: Functionally or locally: progesterone's action in the myometrium is reduced while blood levels stay high. No single human trigger is established.
cards.quote: In humans circulating progesterone stays elevated until birth, so the withdrawal that releases the myometrium is thought to be functional or local rather than systemic
cards.section: Labour: lifting progesterone's block

cards.front: In sheep, how is progesterone's block on the uterus lifted near term?
cards.back: A rise in fetal adrenal cortisol shifts the placenta's steroid output away from progesterone toward estrogens and prostaglandins, so progesterone itself falls.
cards.quote: a rise in fetal adrenal cortisol near term shifts the placenta's steroid output away from progesterone and toward estrogens and prostaglandins
cards.section: Labour: lifting progesterone's block

cards.front: Near term, what two things does the myometrium gain that let it respond to oxytocin and contract as one?
cards.back: Oxytocin receptors and gap junctions, which link its cells so they contract together.
cards.quote: Near term the myometrium gains oxytocin receptors and gap junctions, which link its cells so they contract together.
cards.section: Labour: lifting progesterone's block

cards.front: In labour, what two actions do prostaglandins have?
cards.back: They contract the myometrium and soften the cervical stroma.
cards.quote: Prostaglandins contract the myometrium and soften the cervical stroma.
cards.section: Labour: lifting progesterone's block

cards.front: Describe the positive-feedback loop that oxytocin drives in labour.
cards.back: Stretch of the cervix and vagina can release oxytocin; oxytocin strengthens uterine contraction; stronger contraction increases stretch.
cards.quote: Stretch of the cervix and vagina can release oxytocin, oxytocin increases uterine contraction, and stronger contraction increases stretch
cards.section: Labour: lifting progesterone's block

cards.front: Mice lacking oxytocin deliver without obvious deficits, yet their pups are not nursed. What do the two results show about oxytocin's jobs?
cards.back: Labour, in mice at least, does not depend on oxytocin; milk ejection does. The milk is made but not ejected, which fits prolactin fills, oxytocin empties.
cards.quote: they fail to nurse their pups, because the milk is made but not ejected
cards.section: Milk: prolactin fills, oxytocin empties

cards.front: In lactation, where is prolactin made and what does it do?
cards.back: In the anterior pituitary; it supports secretion of milk by the alveolar cells of the breast.
cards.quote: Prolactin, from the anterior pituitary, supports secretion of milk by the alveolar cells of the breast
cards.section: Milk: prolactin fills, oxytocin empties

cards.front: In lactation, where is oxytocin released and what does it do?
cards.back: From the posterior pituitary; it contracts the myoepithelial cells around each alveolus and ejects milk already stored. Suckling, and cues such as crying, release it.
cards.quote: contracts the myoepithelial cells wrapped around each alveolus and ejects milk already stored
cards.section: Milk: prolactin fills, oxytocin empties

cards.front: A nursing mother's prolactin is suppressed, but her oxytocin response to suckling is intact. Predict milk ejection now and milk supply over the following days.
cards.back: Stored milk can still be ejected at first, because oxytocin empties the alveolus. Secretion falls, so supply dwindles, because prolactin fills it.
cards.quote: Milk has two hormones with two jobs, and students reverse them.
cards.section: Milk: prolactin fills, oxytocin empties

cards.front: Prolactin is high by late pregnancy. Why does full milk production wait until two to three days after birth?
cards.back: Progesterone from the placenta appears to restrain the switch. After birth the placenta is gone; progesterone falls with prolactin maintained, permitting secretory activation.
cards.quote: the fall in progesterone, with prolactin maintained, permits the switch, two to three days after birth
cards.section: Milk: prolactin fills, oxytocin empties

cards.front: After delivery, a fragment of placenta that keeps making progesterone stays in the uterus. Predict the effect on the onset of full milk production, and name the rule.
cards.back: Secretory activation is likely delayed, because progesterone appears to restrain the switch even with prolactin high. Rule: the hormone that keeps the uterus quiet keeps the breast waiting.
cards.quote: The same hormone that keeps the uterus quiet keeps the breast waiting.
cards.section: Milk: prolactin fills, oxytocin empties

cards.front: Suppose a drug crossing the placenta blocked fetal prostaglandin E2 synthesis late in pregnancy, and the ductus arteriosus constricted before birth. Where would right ventricular output have to go, and what would it meet?
cards.back: Into the pulmonary artery and through the fluid-filled lungs, a high-resistance bed. Prostaglandin E2 mainly holds the fetal ductus open (nitric oxide also contributes); without the shunt, flow cannot bypass the lungs.
cards.why: Rests on two stated rules: PGE2 keeps the ductus open, and fetal lungs are the hard bed.
cards.quote: Prostaglandin E2 holds the fetal ductus arteriosus open predominantly by acting on EP4 receptors
cards.section: Closing the ductus
